lessons.title: Welcome to Python
lessons.description: Your first steps into the world of Python programming

theorySlides.title: What is Python? 🐍
theorySlides.content:
Python is one of the world's most popular programming languages. It's used by companies like Google, Netflix, and Instagram to build amazing software.

Python is known for being:
• Easy to read and write
• Powerful yet simple
• Perfect for beginners
• Used everywhere: web development, data science, AI, and more!

theorySlides.title: Why Choose Python?
theorySlides.content:
Python was designed to be simple and readable. Unlike other programming languages that use lots of symbols and brackets, Python uses plain English words.

Python powers:
🌐 Websites (Instagram, Pinterest)
🤖 AI and Machine Learning (Tesla, Spotify)
📊 Data Analysis (Netflix recommendations)
🎮 Games (Civilization IV)

theorySlides.title: Your First Python Program
theorySlides.content: Every programmer starts with "Hello, World!" - a simple program that displays text on the screen.
theorySlides.codeSnippet: print("Hello, World!")

questions.question: What makes Python special compared to other programming languages?
options: It's easy to read and write
questions.explanation: Python's main strength is its readability and simplicity, making it perfect for beginners while still being powerful enough for experts.

questions.question: Which command displays text in Python?
questions.explanation: The print() function is used to display text output in Python.

questions.question: What punctuation must surround text in print()?
questions.explanation: Text (strings) in Python must be wrapped in quotes - either single '' or double "".

questions.question: Which company uses Python?
questions.explanation: Python is used by many major companies including Google, Netflix, Instagram, Spotify, and more!

codingChallenge.title: Say Hello!
codingChallenge.description: Write a program that displays "Hello, Python!" to the screen.
codingChallenge.hint: Use the print() function to display text. Remember to put your text in quotes!

lessons.title: Variables - Storing Information
lessons.description: Learn how to store and use data in your programs

theorySlides.title: What are Variables? 📦
theorySlides.content:
Think of variables like labeled boxes that store information. You can put different types of data in these boxes and use them later.

For example:
• A box labeled "name" might contain "Alice"
• A box labeled "age" might contain 25
• A box labeled "is_student" might contain True

theorySlides.title: Creating Variables
theorySlides.content: In Python, creating a variable is super simple! You just write the name, an equals sign, and the value.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
name = "Alex"
age = 20
height = 5.8
is_student = True

theorySlides.title: Types of Data
theorySlides.content:
Python automatically understands different types of data:

• Text (String): "Hello", "Python", "123 Main St"
• Numbers (Integer): 5, 42, -10, 0
• Decimal Numbers (Float): 3.14, 2.5, -1.2
• True/False (Boolean): True, False
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
message = "Welcome!"  # Text
score = 100          # Whole number
price = 19.99        # Decimal
is_open = True       # True/False

theorySlides.title: Using Variables
theorySlides.content: Once you create a variable, you can use it anywhere in your program by writing its name.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
player_name = "Maya"
points = 150

print("Player:", player_name)
print("Points:", points)
print("Great job", player_name, "!")

questions.question: How do you create a variable called "score" with the value 100?
questions.explanation: In Python, you create variables using the assignment operator (=). Just write: score = 100

questions.question: What type of data is "Hello World"?
questions.explanation: Text in quotes is called a String. "Hello World" is a string because it contains text characters.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: Variable names can contain letters, numbers, and underscores, but cannot start with a number or contain hyphens.

questions.question: What is the value of x after: x = 5; x = 10?
questions.explanation: Variables can be reassigned. The second assignment (x = 10) replaces the first value.

questions.question: What type is the value True?
questions.explanation: True and False are Boolean values - they represent yes/no or on/off states.

lessons.title: Math in Python
lessons.description: Learn to do calculations and work with numbers

theorySlides.title: Python is a Great Calculator! 🔢
theorySlides.content: Python can perform all basic math operations and much more. You can use it like a powerful calculator!
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
print(5 + 3)    # Addition: 8
print(10 - 4)   # Subtraction: 6
print(6 * 7)    # Multiplication: 42
print(15 / 3)   # Division: 5.0

theorySlides.title: Math with Variables
theorySlides.content: You can use variables in math operations, making your calculations dynamic and reusable.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
price = 25
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity

print("Total cost:", total)  # Total cost: 75

theorySlides.title: Special Math Operations
theorySlides.content: Python has some special math operators that are really useful:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
print(10 ** 2)   # Power: 10 squared = 100
print(17 // 5)   # Floor division: 3
print(17 % 5)    # Modulo (remainder): 2

theorySlides.title: Updating Variables
theorySlides.content: You can change a variable's value by assigning it a new value. You can even use the variable's current value to calculate the new one!
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
score = 100
print("Current score:", score)

score = score + 50  # Add 50 points
print("New score:", score)

# Shortcut: score += 50 does the same thing

questions.question: What does 10 ** 3 equal in Python?
questions.explanation: ** is the power operator. 10 ** 3 means 10 to the power of 3, which is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

questions.question: If x = 5, what will x += 3 make x equal to?
questions.explanation: x += 3 is shorthand for x = x + 3. So if x starts at 5, it becomes 5 + 3 = 8.

questions.question: What does the % operator do?
questions.explanation: The % operator (modulo) returns the remainder after division. For example, 17 % 5 = 2.

questions.question: What is 15 // 4 in Python?
questions.explanation: // is floor division - it divides and rounds down to the nearest whole number. 15 / 4 = 3.75, but 15 // 4 = 3.

questions.question: Which operator has the highest priority (executes first)?
questions.explanation: Python follows math order of operations: ** (power) is calculated first, then * and /, then + and -.

lessons.title: Working with Text
lessons.description: Master text manipulation and string operations

theorySlides.title: Strings are Powerful! 📝
theorySlides.content: In programming, text is called a "string" because it's like a string of characters tied together. Python has many tools to work with text.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
message = "Hello, World!"
name = "Python"
sentence = "Learning " + name + " is fun!"

theorySlides.title: Combining Text (Concatenation)
theorySlides.content: You can join strings together using the + operator, just like adding numbers!
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
first_name = "John"
last_name = "Doe"
full_name = first_name + " " + last_name

print(full_name)  # John Doe

theorySlides.title: Useful String Methods
theorySlides.content: Strings come with built-in "methods" - special functions that can transform them:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
text = "Hello World"

print(text.upper())     # HELLO WORLD
print(text.lower())     # hello world
print(text.title())     # Hello World
print(len(text))        # 11 (length)

theorySlides.title: F-strings: The Modern Way
theorySlides.content: F-strings are the most elegant way to combine text and variables in Python:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
name = "Alice"
age = 30
score = 95.5

# Old way:
message1 = "Hi " + name + ", you are " + str(age)

# F-string way (modern):
message2 = f"Hi {name}, you are {age} years old!"
message3 = f"Your score is {score}%"

questions.question: How do you combine "Hello" and "World" with a space between?
questions.explanation: To combine strings with a space, use: "Hello" + " " + "World" which gives "Hello World".

questions.question: What does "python".upper() return?
questions.explanation: The .upper() method converts all letters to uppercase, so "python" becomes "PYTHON".

questions.question: Which is an f-string?
questions.explanation: F-strings start with f and use {variable_name} syntax: f"Hello {name}"

questions.question: What does len("Python") return?
questions.explanation: len() returns the number of characters in a string. "Python" has 6 characters.

questions.question: How do you get the first character of text = "Hello"?
questions.explanation: Use square brackets with index. In Python, indexing starts at 0, so text[0] is the first character.

codingChallenge.title: Build a Username
codingChallenge.description: Create a username by combining first name, last name initial, and birth year.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
first_name = "john"
last_name = "doe"
birth_year = 1995

# Create username: firstname + first letter of lastname + year
# Example: john + d + 1995 = "johnd1995"
username = 

print(username)
codingChallenge.hint: Use string concatenation (+) or an f-string. To get the first letter of last_name, use last_name[0]. Convert birth_year to string with str().
codingChallenge.solution:

last_name = "doe"
birth_year = 1995

username = first_name + last_name[0] + str(birth_year)
print(username)

lessons.title: Making Decisions
lessons.description: Learn how programs make choices using if statements

theorySlides.title: Programs That Think! 🤔
theorySlides.content:
Real programs need to make decisions based on different situations. The "if" statement lets your program choose what to do.

Think of it like:
"IF it's raining, bring an umbrella"
"IF the score is high, show congratulations"

theorySlides.title: Basic If Statement
theorySlides.content: The if statement checks if something is true, then runs code only if it is:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
age = 18

if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote!")
    print("Welcome to adulthood!")

print("This always runs")

theorySlides.title: If-Else: Two Choices
theorySlides.content: Use else to handle the case when the condition is false:

theorySlides.title: Multiple Conditions
theorySlides.content: Use elif (else if) to check multiple conditions:

theorySlides.title: Comparison Operators
theorySlides.content: These operators help you compare values:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
# Comparison operators
print(5 == 5)    # Equal to: True
print(5 != 3)    # Not equal: True
print(7 > 5)     # Greater than: True
print(4 < 8)     # Less than: True
print(5 >= 5)    # Greater or equal: True
print(3 <= 10)   # Less or equal: True

questions.question: What happens if the condition in an if statement is false?
options: The code inside the if block is skipped
questions.explanation: When an if condition is false, Python skips all the code inside that if block.

questions.question: What does the == operator do?
options: Checks if two values are equal
questions.explanation: == checks if two values are equal and returns True or False. Don't confuse it with = which assigns values.

questions.question: Which keyword is used for "otherwise" in Python?
questions.explanation: The "else" keyword handles the case when the if condition is false.

questions.question: What happens if no condition is True and there is no else?
questions.explanation: If no condition matches and there is no else block, Python simply skips the entire if statement.

questions.question: Which operator means "not equal"?
questions.explanation: != checks if two values are NOT equal. Example: 5 != 3 returns True.

codingChallenge.starterCode:

lessons.title: Working with Lists
lessons.description: Learn to store multiple items in ordered collections

theorySlides.title: What are Lists? 📝
theorySlides.content:
Lists let you store multiple items in a single variable. They are ordered, changeable, and allow duplicate values.

Real-world examples:
• Shopping list
• Playlist of songs
• List of high scores
• Todo items

theorySlides.title: Creating Lists
theorySlides.content: Lists are created using square brackets [], with items separated by commas.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
mixed = [1, "hello", True, 3.14]

print(fruits)

theorySlides.title: Accessing List Items
theorySlides.content: Access items by their index number. Python uses zero-based indexing (first item is 0).
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]

print(fruits[0])   # apple
print(fruits[1])   # banana
print(fruits[-1])  # cherry (last item)

theorySlides.title: List Methods
theorySlides.content: Python provides many built-in methods to modify lists.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]

# Add item
fruits.append("cherry")

# Remove item
fruits.remove("banana")

# Sort list
fruits.sort()

print(fruits)

questions.question: Which index accesses the first element?
questions.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing: index 0 is the first element.

questions.question: Which method adds an item to the end?
questions.explanation: append() adds a single item to the end of a list.

questions.question: What does fruits[-1] return if fruits = ["a", "b", "c"]?
questions.explanation: Negative indexing starts from the end. -1 is the last item, -2 is second to last, etc.

questions.question: How do you change the second item in a list?
questions.explanation: The second item has index 1 (since indexing starts at 0). Use list[1] = value to change it.

lessons.title: Loops and Iteration
lessons.description: Repeat actions efficiently with for and while loops

theorySlides.title: The for Loop 🔄
theorySlides.content: Loops let you repeat code multiple times. The for loop iterates over sequences.

theorySlides.title: The range() Function
theorySlides.content: range() generates sequences of numbers for loops.

theorySlides.title: The while Loop
theorySlides.content: while loops continue as long as a condition is True.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1  # Important!

questions.question: What does range(3) generate?
questions.explanation: range(3) generates 0, 1, 2 (up to but not including 3).

questions.question: Which keyword exits a loop?
questions.explanation: break immediately exits the current loop.

questions.question: What does range(2, 8, 2) generate?
questions.explanation: range(2, 8, 2) starts at 2, ends before 8, step 2 → gives 2, 4, 6.

questions.question: Which keyword skips to the next iteration?
questions.explanation: continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one.

questions.question: What is wrong with: while True: print("Hi")?
questions.explanation: Since the condition is always True, this loop never stops - it is an infinite loop!

codingChallenge.title: Print Even Numbers
codingChallenge.description: Print all even numbers from 0 to 10.

theorySlides.title: What are Dictionaries? 🗂️
theorySlides.content:
Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs. Each key is unique and maps to a value.

Like a real dictionary:
Word (key) → Definition (value)

In programming:
"name" → "Alice"
"age" → 25

theorySlides.title: Creating Dictionaries
theorySlides.content: Use curly braces {} with key:value pairs.

theorySlides.title: Dictionary Methods
theorySlides.content: Useful methods for working with dictionaries.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}

# Get all keys
print(person.keys())

# Get all values
print(person.values())

# Check if key exists
if "name" in person:
    print("Found!")

questions.question: How do you access a dictionary value?
questions.explanation: Use bracket notation: dict["key"].

questions.question: Which method returns all keys?
questions.explanation: The keys() method returns all dictionary keys.

questions.question: What happens if you access a key that does not exist?
questions.explanation: Accessing a non-existent key raises a KeyError. Use .get("key") to safely return None instead.

questions.question: Can dictionary keys be lists?
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be immutable (unchangeable). Lists can change, so they cannot be keys.

codingChallenge.title: Student Record
codingChallenge.description: Create a dictionary with name, age, grade. Print the name.

theorySlides.title: What are Functions? ⚙️
theorySlides.content:
Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform specific tasks.

Benefits:
• Avoid code repetition
• Organize complex programs
• Make code easier to test
• Enable code sharing

theorySlides.title: Defining Functions
theorySlides.content: Use the def keyword to create functions.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
def greet():
    print("Hello!")

# Call the function
greet()
greet()  # Can call multiple times

theorySlides.title: Function Parameters
theorySlides.content: Functions can accept input values (parameters).
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Alice")
greet("Bob")

theorySlides.title: Return Values
theorySlides.content: Functions can return values using return.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(5, 3)
print(result)  # 8

questions.question: What keyword defines a function?
questions.explanation: The def keyword defines functions in Python.

questions.question: What does a function return by default?
questions.explanation: Functions without return statements return None.

questions.question: What is wrong with: def greet(name): return f"Hi {name}" print("Done")?
questions.explanation: return exits the function immediately. Code after return is unreachable.

questions.question: What are parameters?
questions.explanation: Parameters are variables that receive values when the function is called.

lessons.title: Handling Errors
lessons.description: Deal with errors gracefully in your code

theorySlides.title: What are Exceptions? ⚠️
theorySlides.content:
Exceptions are errors that occur during program execution.

Common exceptions:
• ZeroDivisionError (divide by 0)
• ValueError (wrong value type)
• TypeError (wrong data type)
• FileNotFoundError (missing file)

theorySlides.title: Try and Except
theorySlides.content: Handle errors with try/except blocks to prevent crashes.

theorySlides.title: Multiple Exceptions
theorySlides.content: Handle different error types separately.

theorySlides.title: Finally Block
theorySlides.content: Code in finally always runs, whether an error occurred or not.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
try:
    file = open("data.txt")
    # Do something
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found!")
finally:
    print("Cleanup complete")

questions.question: Which block handles exceptions?
questions.explanation: The except block catches and handles exceptions.

questions.question: When does the finally block execute?
questions.explanation: finally always executes, regardless of errors.

questions.question: What exception occurs when dividing by zero?
questions.explanation: ZeroDivisionError is raised when you try to divide a number by zero.

questions.question: How do you catch any exception?
questions.explanation: except Exception: catches most exceptions. You can also use except: alone to catch all.

codingChallenge.starterCode:
